stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
When the state of Ardena raised its minimum wage by 12 percent in 2019, economist Lena Osei tracked payrolls at 900 restaurants and found no drop in staffing over the following two years. Osei concluded that moderate minimum wage increases do not reduce employment.

Text 2
Osei's restaurant data are careful, but most of those restaurants were in cities, where pay already exceeded the old minimum. In rural counties, where many workers earned exactly the minimum, a similar increase could push employers to cut hours or positions.
choices: It offers further evidence that moderate wage increases leave employment unchanged.
It argues that Text 1's conclusion may not hold in areas unlike those mostly studied.
It presents a finding about rural employers that Text 1 then attempts to explain.
It claims that the payroll records in Text 1 were gathered using flawed methods.
explanation: Text 1 ends with a broad conclusion: moderate increases don't reduce employment. Text 2 grants that the data are careful ("careful, but"), then points out that the sample was mostly urban and suggests that rural counties, where many workers earned exactly the minimum, could respond differently. It narrows where Text 1's conclusion applies without rejecting the finding, so B is right.

A.why: You took Text 2's opening praise for its whole point. After "but," Text 2 suggests that employment could fall in rural counties. That raises a doubt about Text 1's conclusion and doesn't support it.

C.why: You reversed the direction. Text 1 never mentions rural employers and explains nothing Text 2 raises. Text 2 is the one responding to Text 1.

D.why: You made Text 2's objection stronger than it is. Text 2 calls Osei's data "careful" and only questions how far the results extend. It never says the records were gathered badly.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
After the city of Marlow converted several downtown traffic lanes to bus and bicycle lanes in 2017, hospital admissions for childhood asthma in nearby neighborhoods fell by 18 percent within three years. A team of epidemiologists concluded that reduced vehicle emissions produced the improvement.

Text 2
No one disputes that asthma admissions in Marlow dropped. But in 2017 the county also began sending nurses into the homes of children with asthma to teach families to use inhalers correctly. It is difficult to exclude that program as the source of the decline.
choices: It questions whether asthma admissions in Marlow actually declined as Text 1 reports.
It extends the finding in Text 1 to respiratory illnesses other than asthma.
It describes a home-visit program that Text 1 credits for the drop in admissions.
It accepts the decline reported in Text 1 but offers another possible cause for it.
explanation: Text 1 reports a decline and attributes it to lower emissions. Text 2 opens by accepting the decline ("No one disputes...") and then names a nurse home-visit program that began the same year and "could" explain the result. It keeps the observation and offers a different explanation, which is D.

A.why: You missed the concession. Text 2 says outright that "no one disputes" the drop. It questions the cause, not whether the decline happened.

B.why: Neither text mentions any illness other than asthma. Text 2 doesn't widen Text 1's finding. It questions the explanation for it.

C.why: You got Text 2's content right but Text 1's role wrong. Text 1 credits reduced vehicle emissions and never mentions the home-visit program. Text 2 introduces the program as a rival explanation.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Professional observatories schedule their telescopes months in advance and rarely watch one object for long. Amateur astronomers, by contrast, can monitor a single target night after night. That patience increasingly lets amateurs record brief events that professionals would otherwise miss.

Text 2
In 2021, retired teacher Ines Varga was filming Jupiter from her backyard when a bright flash appeared on the planet's cloud tops for under two seconds. No professional instrument was aimed at Jupiter then, and her footage let researchers estimate the size of the object that struck it.
choices: It describes a specific case that illustrates the general point made in Text 1.
It argues that professional observatories are less precise than Text 1 suggests.
It states a general claim that Text 1 supports by offering a particular case.
It shifts attention from amateur observers to the size of objects striking Jupiter.
explanation: Text 1 makes a general claim: because amateurs can watch one target for a long time, they catch brief events professionals miss. Text 2 tells one such story: an amateur filmed a two-second flash on Jupiter while no professional instrument was aimed at it. Text 2 is a specific example of Text 1's general point, so A is right.

B.why: Neither text says anything about how precise professional instruments are. Text 1's point is about scheduling and attention, and Text 2 says only that no professional telescope was aimed at Jupiter.

C.why: You swapped the roles. Text 1 is the general claim and Text 2 is the particular case. This choice describes the relationship in reverse.

D.why: You latched onto a detail. The size estimate appears only at the end to show what Varga's footage made possible. Text 2 is still about an amateur catching an event.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Seismologist Rafael Duarte examined 40 major earthquakes along the Kessar subduction zone and found that 28 were preceded, days or weeks earlier, by clusters of small tremors known as foreshock swarms. Duarte therefore suggests that monitoring such swarms could give coastal communities advance warning.

Text 2
Duarte's pattern is real, but it looks only backward from large earthquakes. Looking forward, the Kessar zone produced more than 300 swarms over the same period, and nearly all of them faded without a major quake. A warning system based on swarms would mostly sound false alarms.
choices: It reports that the large earthquakes in Text 1 were rarely preceded by swarms.
It proposes a more reliable method of forecasting large earthquakes than swarms.
It accepts the pattern in Text 1 but disputes the practical use Text 1 proposes.
It presents a warning proposal that Text 1 goes on to test with earthquake records.
explanation: Text 1 builds from evidence (28 of 40 quakes had foreshock swarms) to a final proposal marked by "therefore": monitor swarms to warn communities. Text 2 grants the pattern ("is real, but") and then answers that final proposal: most swarms are never followed by a major quake, so a warning system would mostly sound false alarms. C captures both halves.

A.why: Text 2 accepts that 28 of the 40 quakes followed swarms. Its point runs the other way: most swarms aren't followed by quakes. It doesn't say most quakes lacked swarms.

B.why: Text 2 criticizes the swarm-based approach but never offers a replacement. Nothing in it describes another forecasting method.

D.why: You got the direction wrong. The warning proposal comes from Text 1, and Text 2 responds to it. Text 1 doesn't test anything that Text 2 proposes.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In the 1880s, collector Owen Pryce transcribed dozens of tales from storytellers in the hill villages of Gwennol. Because he recorded tellings made before radio and schooling reached the region, his volumes should serve as the standard for those tales; later versions that depart from them reflect a tradition in decline.

Text 2
Pryce's volumes are an invaluable record. Yet when I recorded Gwennol storytellers last decade, the same teller would lengthen a tale for children and sharpen its jokes for adults. Such variation is not decay; it is how an oral tale stays alive.
choices: It argues that Pryce's volumes are inaccurate records of nineteenth-century tellings.
It values the records in Text 1 but rejects using them to judge later tellings as decline.
It agrees with Text 1 that recent Gwennol tellings show a tradition in decline.
It offers a fixed version of each tale that Text 1 then adopts as the standard.
explanation: Text 1 ends on its claim: Pryce's volumes should be the standard, and departures from them mean the tradition is declining. Text 2 credits the volumes ("an invaluable record") and then argues that variation "is not decay." It accepts the records but challenges the conclusion Text 1 draws from them, which is B.

A.why: Text 2 calls Pryce's volumes "an invaluable record" and never questions their accuracy. It objects to treating them as the standard, not to what they contain.

C.why: This reverses Text 2's position. It says directly that variation "is not decay," so it rejects the decline view.

D.why: You reversed the roles. The fixed standard comes from Text 1, through Pryce, and Text 2 argues against fixing tales at all. Text 1 adopts nothing from Text 2.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Weaving accounts from one northern English district show that, after 1790, households using a newly introduced treadle loom wove nearly twice as much cloth per week as households still using older frames. Historian Mara Lindqvist therefore concludes that the new loom drove the district's surge in cloth output.

Text 2
Lindqvist's weekly figures are not in doubt. But the households that took up the loom were mostly those already contracted to merchants who supplied them with yarn year-round. A steady supply of yarn alone could have raised their output, and the accounts cannot rule that out.
choices: Households using the new loom wove more cloth each week than households using older frames.
The new loom was the main reason the district's cloth output rose after 1790.
A reliable supply of yarn did more than any loom to raise the district's output.
The district's weaving accounts are too incomplete to show how much cloth was woven.
explanation: Text 1 reports that loom households wove nearly twice as much cloth per week and concludes the loom caused the surge. Text 2 opens by accepting those weekly figures ('not in doubt') and then offers a different explanation for them. What Text 2 grants is what both authors share: households with the new loom wove more cloth each week.

B.why: You took Text 1's conclusion as common ground. That causal claim is exactly what Text 2 disputes when it says yarn supply could explain the gains, so only Text 1 holds this view.

C.why: You read Text 2's possible explanation as a firm claim, and as one both authors hold. Text 2 says yarn 'could have' raised output, not that it mattered more, and Lindqvist credits the loom.

D.why: Neither author says this. Text 2 says the accounts cannot rule out one explanation, but both authors accept the weekly output figures the accounts provide.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After a national weather service added 400 automated ground stations to its network, its three-day rainfall forecasts for the country's plains became markedly more accurate. Meteorologist Daniel Osei concludes that denser station networks improve rainfall forecasts wherever they are installed.

Text 2
Osei is right that forecasts for the plains improved. In steep mountain valleys, however, the new stations made little difference. Storms there are set off by ridges and slopes far smaller than the forecast model can represent, so more measurements cannot fix what the model is unable to see.
choices: Denser station networks improve rainfall forecasts in every type of terrain.
Forecast errors in mountain valleys come mainly from having too few stations.
The added stations made three-day rainfall forecasts for the plains more accurate.
Forecast models should be redesigned before any more stations are installed.
explanation: Text 1 reports better forecasts for the plains and then broadens that into a claim about everywhere. Text 2 accepts the plains result ('Osei is right') but names one kind of place, mountain valleys, where the claim fails. Text 2 narrows Text 1's claim without rejecting it, so what both accept is the plains result.

A.why: You took Text 1's final conclusion as shared. Text 2 was written to challenge exactly that 'wherever they are installed' claim, using mountain valleys as the counterexample.

B.why: This reverses Text 2. It says valley errors come from terrain features too small for the model, and that extra stations did not help.

D.why: Neither author recommends this. Text 2 points out a limit of the model, but it never says installation should stop or wait.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a ten-week trial, adults who ate six servings of fermented foods daily showed a greater rise in gut microbial diversity than adults who ate a high-fiber diet. Nutrition researcher Hana Okafor concludes that fermented foods are the more effective way to diversify the gut microbiome.

Text 2
Although diversity did climb faster in the fermented-food group, ten weeks may be too short to judge fiber fairly. The microbes that break down fiber can take months to become established in the gut, so fiber's effects may simply arrive later than the trial measured.
choices: A high-fiber diet does not increase gut microbial diversity at all.
Over the ten-week trial, diversity rose more in the fermented-food group.
Fermented foods are the better long-term way to diversify gut microbes.
Fiber's benefits for the gut always appear only after several months.
explanation: Text 1 reports the trial result and concludes fermented foods work better. Text 2 begins with a concession ('Although diversity did climb faster in the fermented-food group') and then questions whether ten weeks was long enough. The concession is the shared ground: within the trial, the fermented-food group gained more diversity.

A.why: You pushed the trial result too far. Text 1 says only that fiber produced a smaller rise, and Text 2 suggests fiber's effects may come later. Neither says fiber does nothing.

C.why: Text 1 holds this view, but Text 2 is written to doubt it. You got Text 1's position right and assumed Text 2 shared it.

D.why: This states Text 2's guarded 'may' as a certainty. Okafor, whose conclusion depends on the ten-week result, would not accept it either.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a trial with forty competitive distance runners, those who held static stretches for ten minutes before a 1,500-meter time trial finished an average of four seconds slower than when they skipped stretching. Exercise physiologist Lena Hartmann concludes that athletes in any sport should avoid static stretching before competing.

Text 2
Hartmann's result fits what is known about runners, whose strides rely on stiff tendons that store and release energy. Gymnasts are a different case. Their routines demand extreme flexibility, and in trials by sports scientist Rafael Ortiz, they scored higher after stretching than without it.
choices: Static stretching before competition harms performance in every sport.
Gymnasts benefit from stretching because their tendons are especially stiff.
The runners' slower times came from fatigue rather than from stretching.
The runners in the trial ran more slowly after stretching than without it.
explanation: Text 1 reports slower times for runners after stretching and then extends that into advice for every sport. Text 2 accepts the runner result ('fits what is known about runners') but offers gymnasts as a group where it does not hold. Because Text 2 limits the claim rather than denying the finding, the runner result is what both authors accept.

A.why: This is Text 1's broad conclusion, and Text 2 exists to narrow it. You got Text 1's role right and missed that Text 2 limits it to runners.

B.why: This mixes up Text 2's details. It is runners who rely on stiff tendons, while gymnasts are described as needing extreme flexibility.

C.why: Neither text offers fatigue as an explanation. Text 2 does not question the runner result at all. It questions only whether that result applies to every sport.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Images of a remote galaxy cluster show that its member galaxies emit light far redder than models of young, star-forming galaxies predict. Because aging populations of stars grow steadily redder, astronomer Priya Natarajan concludes that star formation in the cluster ended unusually early.

Text 2
No one disputes how red these galaxies look. Yet thick clouds of interstellar dust also redden light, scattering blue wavelengths while letting red ones pass. Dusty galaxies that are still forming stars could therefore appear just as red as old, quiet ones.
choices: Star formation in the cluster ended earlier than it did in most galaxies.
Interstellar dust is the reason the cluster's galaxies appear so red.
The cluster's galaxies look redder than models of young galaxies predict.
Aging populations of stars do not become redder as time passes.
explanation: Text 1 observes that the galaxies are unexpectedly red and explains this with aging stars. Text 2 accepts the observation ('No one disputes how red these galaxies look') and proposes a different cause, dust. The two authors share the observation but not the explanation, so the observation is what both would agree with.

A.why: This is Natarajan's conclusion, the claim Text 2 challenges. You assumed Text 2 accepted the conclusion when it accepts only the observation.

B.why: This states Text 2's possibility as a fact. Text 2 says dust 'could' explain the color, and Natarajan credits aging stars instead.

D.why: Text 1 relies on the opposite idea, and Text 2 never questions how stars age. Text 2 adds a second cause of reddening without denying the first.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which one?
stimulus:
Text 1
Researchers studying a coastal fishing village found that younger residents had largely stopped using a regional vowel sound that their grandparents used. Teenagers in the village spend hours each day watching streamed video in the standard dialect. The researchers therefore concluded that exposure to broadcast media is driving the loss of the vowel.

Text 2
Media exposure has certainly grown in such villages, and the decline of the vowel is well documented. Over the same decades, however, the village cannery closed, and many families began commuting to a nearby city for work. There they talk face to face with speakers of the standard dialect every day. Face-to-face contact is known to shift pronunciation, so it is difficult to rule it out as the cause.
choices: Younger villagers use the regional vowel less often than older villagers did.
Teenagers in the village regularly hear the standard dialect through media.
Broadcast media is the most likely cause of the regional vowel's decline.
A change in how a community speaks can be traced to a social cause.
explanation: Write down both positions. Author 1 thinks media exposure is causing the vowel's loss. Author 2 thinks the loss is real but that face-to-face contact at work could just as well explain it. Author 2 grants the observation and offers another mechanism, so they don't accept that media is the most likely cause. Only Author 1 holds that view, so C is the statement both authors would NOT agree with.

A.why: You may have read Text 2 as rejecting Text 1 outright. But Text 2 calls the vowel's decline 'well documented,' so both authors accept this observation. A statement they share can't be the exception.

B.why: You probably took Text 2's argument against media as a denial that media exposure exists. Text 2 opens by granting it: 'Media exposure has certainly grown.' The concession marks this as common ground.

D.why: You looked at the two different causes and concluded that the authors disagree about causes in general. Each author names a social cause, media for one and workplace contact for the other. So both accept that speech change can have a social cause. They only disagree about which one.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which one?
stimulus:
Text 1
Many migratory songbirds in North America now reach their breeding grounds earlier than they did fifty years ago. Ecologist Mara Lindqvist analyzed banding records for 40 species and found that arrival dates moved earlier as spring temperatures rose. She concluded that migratory songbirds as a group are adjusting their timing to a warming climate.

Text 2
Lindqvist's records show a real trend, but most of them come from short-distance migrants that winter in the southern United States. Long-distance migrants that winter in South America cannot sense northern spring conditions before they depart. Studies of several such species show little change in arrival dates. For these birds, the warming signal may simply arrive too late to act on.
choices: Spring conditions at northern breeding grounds have warmed in recent decades.
Many songbirds reach their breeding grounds earlier than they once did.
Lindqvist's banding records reveal a genuine shift in arrival timing.
Migratory songbirds as a whole are adjusting their arrival to warming.
explanation: Text 1 ends with its broadest claim, that songbirds 'as a group' are tracking the warming. Text 2 accepts the trend but limits its scope. Long-distance migrants show little change, so the claim doesn't hold for the whole group. Author 2 would reject 'as a whole,' which makes D the exception.

A.why: You may have taken Text 2's doubt about the birds as doubt about the warming itself. Text 2 explains that the 'warming signal' reaches long-distance migrants too late, so it assumes the warming is real. Both authors accept it.

B.why: You treated Text 2 as a flat rejection of Text 1, which is stronger than what it says. Text 2 only narrows the claim. It accepts that many birds, especially short-distance migrants, arrive earlier.

C.why: You overlooked Text 2's concession that Lindqvist's records 'show a real trend.' Author 2 questions how far the data extend, not whether they are valid. That makes this statement shared ground.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with each of the following statements EXCEPT which one?
stimulus:
Text 1
The city of Harlow Bay converted the parking lanes on three downtown blocks into protected bike lanes. Within two years, sales at shops on those blocks rose 12 percent. City planners cited the result as evidence that removing street parking need not hurt nearby businesses. They suggested that the lanes may even help by bringing in cyclists, who tend to stop at shops more often than drivers do.

Text 2
No one disputes the rise in sales on those blocks. During the same period, however, a 400-unit apartment complex opened one block away, adding hundreds of residents who walk to nearby shops. That growth alone could have raised sales, so it remains uncertain how much the bike lanes contributed.
choices: Sales at shops on the converted blocks increased after the bike lanes opened.
The bike lanes were the main reason that sales on those blocks went up.
The kinds of customers who can easily reach a shop can affect its sales.
The reported rise in sales on those blocks reflects a real change.
explanation: Author 1 thinks the bike lanes helped sales by bringing in cyclists. Author 2 accepts the rise in sales but points out that the new apartment complex could explain it alone. That's the same observation with a different explanation. Author 2 calls the lanes' contribution 'uncertain,' so they would not agree that the lanes were the main reason.

A.why: You may have assumed that because Author 2 doubts the explanation, they also doubt the result. Text 2 says 'No one disputes the rise in sales,' so both authors accept that sales went up.

C.why: You focused on the authors' different customer groups and missed what the two explanations share. Text 1 credits cyclists, and Text 2 credits residents who walk. Both explanations assume that who can reach a shop affects its sales.

D.why: You read Text 2's challenge as an attack on the data. Text 2 explicitly accepts the sales figures and questions only what caused them. Both authors treat the rise as real.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Agronomist Lena Fairweather tracked corn yields on 40 Iowa farms over six seasons. In dry years, fields that had carried a winter cover of cereal rye far outyielded bare fields, apparently because the rye's leftover residue slowed evaporation from the soil. Fairweather concluded that rye's advantage grows as rainfall shrinks.

Text 2
Fairweather's findings on soil moisture are persuasive. Yet in her wet seasons, rye fields barely outyielded bare ones, and on some farms they fell behind, likely because decomposing rye briefly locks up nitrogen that young corn needs. Rye, then, is less a universal booster than a hedge against drought.
choices: Rye-covered fields outyielded bare fields by a similar margin in wet seasons and dry seasons.
The yield gap between rye-covered and bare fields was wider in dry seasons than in wet ones.
Rye cover raises corn yields enough to justify planting it on every farm in every season.
Decomposing rye reduces corn yields by locking up nitrogen that young plants need to grow.
explanation: Write the two sentences first. Author 1 thinks rye helps most when rainfall is low. Author 2 accepts the moisture finding but adds that rye barely helps, and sometimes hurts, in wet seasons. Text 2 qualifies Text 1; it doesn't reject it. Both authors therefore accept that the difference between rye and bare fields is larger in dry years than in wet years. Notice that the question is about the gap between two kinds of season, not about either season alone.

A.why: You missed the comparison both texts make. Text 1 says rye's advantage grows as rain shrinks, and Text 2 says rye barely helped in wet seasons. Both describe an unequal margin, so 'similar' contradicts each of them.

C.why: You took a stronger version of Text 1 and assigned it to both authors. Text 1 never says rye belongs on every farm, and Text 2 says outright that rye is not a universal booster. You got one author's general direction right and the other author's position wrong.

D.why: This is Text 2's explanation alone. Text 1 never mentions nitrogen, so you can't say Author 1 would agree. The question asks for common ground, and you picked one author's claim instead.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
When Lyon's silk workshops adopted the Jacquard loom in the 1810s, a patterned cloth that once required a weaver plus an assistant pulling cords could be woven by the weaver alone. Historian Odile Marchand argues that this halving of labor per loom stripped many households of income and thus deepened poverty in the city's silk districts.

Text 2
Marchand is right that each loom needed fewer hands. But tax rolls show the number of looms in Lyon nearly doubled over the next two decades, so the city's total weaving jobs rose. The cord-pullers did lose work; most weaving households did not.
choices: Operating a Jacquard loom took fewer workers than operating the older patterned loom had.
Most weaving households in Lyon grew poorer in the decades after the Jacquard loom arrived.
The number of looms in Lyon nearly doubled in the decades after the Jacquard loom arrived.
The Jacquard loom removed the need for skilled weavers in Lyon's silk workshops entirely.
explanation: Text 1 ends on its conclusion: fewer workers per loom meant more poverty. Text 2 opens by granting the first half ('Marchand is right that each loom needed fewer hands') and then disputes the second. What the two texts share is in that concession: a Jacquard loom needed fewer workers than the loom it replaced.

B.why: This is the subtype's trap. You took Text 1's conclusion as common ground, but that is exactly the claim Text 2 was written to answer: 'most weaving households did not' lose work.

C.why: This detail appears only in Text 2, as its evidence. Text 1 never discusses how many looms the city had, so you can't say Author 1 agrees with it.

D.why: Neither text says weavers stopped being needed. Both say the weaver kept working and only the assistant was cut. You stretched 'fewer hands' into 'no skilled hands'.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Musicologist Teodor Brandt timed 300 recordings of Beethoven's symphonies made between 1930 and 2010. Those from 1990 to 2010 ran about 12 percent faster, on average, than those from 1930 to 1950. Since the later period saw the rise of period-instrument ensembles, which favored Beethoven's own brisk tempo markings, Brandt concludes that this movement drove the acceleration.

Text 2
Brandt's timings are not in question. But recordings of Brahms and Tchaikovsky, composers the period-instrument movement largely ignored, also sped up over those years. Faster Beethoven could simply reflect a broader shift in taste.
choices: The period-instrument movement is chiefly responsible for faster tempos in Beethoven recordings.
Recordings of Brahms and Tchaikovsky sped up by as much as Beethoven recordings did.
Beethoven recordings from 1990 to 2010 were, on average, faster than those from 1930 to 1950.
Conductors today follow Beethoven's tempo markings more closely than earlier conductors did.
explanation: Text 2 doesn't dispute what Brandt observed ('Brandt's timings are not in question'). It offers a different explanation for that observation. The observation itself is what both accept: later Beethoven recordings ran faster than earlier ones. The authors disagree about why the gap exists, not about whether it exists.

A.why: This is the subtype's trap. This is Text 1's final conclusion, and Text 2 exists to challenge it by offering a broader change in taste as the cause. You got Author 1's view right and Author 2's view wrong.

B.why: Text 2 says only that Brahms and Tchaikovsky recordings 'also sped up'. It never says they sped up by the same amount, and Text 1 doesn't mention them at all. You added an equal-size gap that neither text states.

D.why: Text 1 hints at this through the period ensembles, but Text 2 never addresses how closely conductors follow the markings. A side detail from one text isn't something both authors agree on.
